query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A dual-phase refractory high-entropy alloy (EHEA) that is initially strong yet brittle can be rendered ductile through a controlled high-pressure, high-temperature (HPHT) treatment, which refines its microstructure and creates coherent, discrete precipitates within a continuous matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with an ordered B2 dominant structure embedded in a dual-phase microstructure that currently limits ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply a high-pressure (∼6 GPa) and high-temperature (1200–1500 K) treatment for several hours.
generation.conditions: Ambient to elevated temperature mechanical testing conditions typical of industrial applications, with the alloy subjected to tensile loads.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchically patterned dual-phase microstructure featuring a continuous BCC matrix with discrete, coherent B2 (or similar) precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The HPHT treatment is expected to modify the phase fractions and refine the microstructure, reducing interfacial mismatch and stress concentration. This encourages multiple deformation mechanisms (e.g., dislocation movement, deformation twinning, and transformation-induced plasticity) that work synergistically to improve ductility while maintaining high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will show a marked improvement in tensile ductility (potentially doubling ductility compared to the as-cast state) while preserving high yield strength, overcoming the typical strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.baseline: The untreated EHEA exhibits high strength but limited ductility due to the dominance of brittle ordered phases and inherent interfacial stress concentrations.
generation.boundary: The ductility enhancement is contingent upon achieving a refined, coherent dual-phase microstructure. Deviations in processing parameters (pressure, temperature, or duration) or alloy composition could prevent the desired phase transformations and, thus, the anticipated ductility improvement.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvement in ductility (quantitative change) remains uncertain and may depend on precise processing conditions and composition adjustments. Further experimental validation is required to define the optimal treatment window.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of EHEA samples with identical initial microstructure. Subject one set to the specified HPHT treatment (∼6 GPa, 1200–1500 K for several hours) while keeping a control group untreated. Conduct tensile tests and microstructural characterization (using TEM, XRD, and APT) to assess ductility, phase distribution, and interface coherence.
measurements: Microstructural features (phase fraction, precipitate coherence, grain size)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HPHT-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility (or the expected dual-phase microstructure with coherent interfaces is not observed) compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

Various industrial and advanced functional applications require materials with high strength and ductility. Unfortunately, conventional processing strategies usually attain high material strength at the expense of deteriorated ductility [1] – [3] , whilst developing structures with substantial improvement of both strength and ductility is highly challenging. Recent successes in synthesizing superhard materials [4] – [6] have made the high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment [7] , [8] promising to achieve extreme properties in materials. The combination of pressure and temperature offers the great prospect for altering the microstructure of structural materials that would permit overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off. Given the vast space of control parameters involved in the HPHT treatment and the often complex microstructural evolution under extreme pressures and temperatures [9] , [10] , it remains difficult to predict and interpret the mechanical behaviors of HPHT-treated structural materials, especially the abnormal kinetics and thermodynamics of non-equilibrium interfaces induced by the HPHT treatment [11] , [12] .

decision.trend: Early efforts (2018) focused on refining phase stability in refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) to move from a brittle ordered B2 matrix toward more disordered or dual-phase bcc microstructures with improved ductility. Subsequent work explored interstitial modifications (e.g., N or O) to enhance both ductility and strength at elevated temperatures. More recent studies used stepwise thermomechanical treatments to engineer nanoscale coherent precipitates for ultrahigh strength with good ductility, and high-pressure high-temperature processing was shown to overcome the classic strength-ductility trade-off in an eutectic HEA.
decision.unsolved: While significant progress has been made, achieving robust, high ductility over broad temperature ranges and at large industrial scales remains challenging. Key questions include how to stabilize beneficial phases under varying conditions and how to implement cost-effective, high-throughput processing to tailor microstructures for reproducible ductility.
decision.lever: Apply a high-pressure and high-temperature treatment (e.g., ~6 GPa, 1200–1500 K for several hours) to a dual-phase refractory high-entropy alloy with potential for twinning- and transformation-assisted ductility. This would refine the microstructure and reduce interfacial mismatch, promoting dislocation motion and enhancing plasticity.
decision.why: Building on evidence that carefully tuned hierarchical microstructures and phase fractions can produce a synergy of strength and ductility, an HPHT step can further stabilize and refine the phases, reduce brittle interfaces, and activate multiple deformation mechanisms—leading to improved ductility while maintaining acceptable strength.
